evaluation.positioning_hook: A bipolar inventor fights to keep his mobility aid patent from being stolen, while his own mania, marriage, and sanity become the real battleground.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The underdog-inventor story has a clean emotional promise and a built-in David-vs-Goliath engine, especially once the patent theft and congressional fight kick in. The audience is real, but the script’s legal/process-heavy middle and heavy mental-health material narrow the lane from broad crowd-pleaser to adult prestige drama.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise is easy to state: a volatile inventor builds a life-changing mobility device, then has to fight corporate theft and a rigged system. The hook lands clearly through the Handy Bar, the PTAB fight, and the Capitol climax, though the script takes time to fully reveal the larger political dimension.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Brent is vivid because he’s both inspiring and exhausting: funny onstage, self-destructive offstage, and emotionally legible in the marriage and father-son scenes. Emily and Henry add real counterweight, but Brent remains the engine and the supporting cast is more functional than deeply surprising.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The choice to frame the story through Brent’s inventor-club storytelling gives the script a distinctive performance container and a built-in tonal device. The boldness is strongest in the collision of startup comedy, patent-war procedural, and mental-health breakdown, though some of the later political escalation feels more conventional than the setup.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script has clear escalation points — the pitch, the theft, the PTAB fight, the Capitol rally, the shooting — and those beats keep the story moving. It also spends long stretches in explanatory or repetitive speechifying, which softens urgency between the major set pieces.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The core idea of a damaged inventor fighting for a simple mobility tool is immediately understandable and emotionally sticky. What makes it resonate is the way the personal breakdown and the patent theft mirror each other, even if the script sometimes states that theme more directly than it dramatizes it.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The patent-law, inventor-network, and PTAB worlds feel specific and story-generating, with judges, lawyers, investors, and rival operators creating a real ecosystem around the invention. The script also gives the mobility-impaired user perspective enough texture to make the product feel lived-in rather than abstract.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a recognizable register: wounded, profane, inspirational, and occasionally comic in a way that feels tied to Brent’s voice. The inventor-club monologues give it a signature rhythm, though the tonal shifts into courtroom drama, addiction crisis, and political spectacle are broad enough that the identity can blur at times.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There’s more going on here than a patent dispute: shame, addiction, marriage collapse, class resentment, and the psychology of obsession all sit under the surface. The script keeps returning to the same wound from different angles, which suggests depth, even if some of that depth is delivered in speeches rather than subtext.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Brent/Henry, Brent/Emily, Brent/Jeremy, and Brent/Maximilian all generate usable friction, and the support-group and inventor-club settings create recurring relationship arenas. It’s still fundamentally a lead-driven piece, but the surrounding relationships are strong enough to keep the world from feeling solitary.

lead_characters.name: Brent Woods
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 40s, white, inventor/entrepreneur, married father, bipolar and alcoholic
lead_characters.hook: A charismatic, volatile inventor whose genius is inseparable from his self-destruction. Brent can command a room with humor and conviction, then implode in the next beat; the script tracks him from cocky pitchman to broken husband, courtroom combatant, and finally a man trying to survive his own mind while defending the thing he built.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Bradley Cooper in A Star Is Born — a big, messy, emotionally exposed lead who gets to be funny, magnetic, dangerous, and heartbreaking in the same role. It gives an actor the full-range transformation: public charisma, private collapse, addiction, rage, shame, and redemption.

lead_characters.name: Emily Woods
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 30s-40s, white, wife, mother, working-class, emotionally resilient
lead_characters.hook: Emily is the emotional ballast of the story: the wife who keeps the family afloat, sees through Brent’s chaos, and still keeps choosing love until she can’t. She’s not passive; she’s the one who names the damage, absorbs the fallout, and eventually forces the story to acknowledge the cost of Brent’s obsession.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Laura Linney in The Savages or Michelle Williams in Manchester by the Sea its quiet authority — a woman whose restraint is the performance. It offers a strong actress the chance to play endurance, disappointment, tenderness, and the moment when love becomes a boundary.

lead_characters.name: Henry
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 30s-50s, white, lawyer/business aide, observant, emotionally guarded
lead_characters.hook: Henry is the buffer, translator, and reluctant witness to Brent’s chaos. He starts as the guy cleaning up the mess and ends up as the one person who can speak both legal and emotional truth to Brent without flinching.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded, scene-stealing support role that Paul Dano in There Will Be Blood or Jesse Plemons in The Power of the Dog has turned into a calling card — quiet intelligence under pressure. It gives an actor the chance to play loyalty, fatigue, and moral discomfort without ever becoming ornamental.

lead_characters.name: Maximilian
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 50s, wealthy, corporate operator, polished, predatory
lead_characters.hook: Maximilian is the polished antagonist who understands power as a language and litigation as a weapon. He’s not a cartoon villain; he’s the man who can smile while stripping a smaller inventor of leverage, then pivot into informant mode when the walls close in.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Michael Shannon in Take Shelter or Jeremy Strong in The Trial of the Chicago 7 a chance to weaponize intelligence and menace in equal measure. It’s a deliciously controlled antagonist part with real scene-eating authority.

lead_characters.name: Lizzy
lead_characters.hook: Lizzy is the script’s moral proof point: a woman whose daily struggle with mobility gives the Handy Bar its human stakes. She’s skeptical, funny, and then devastatingly sincere, and her belief in Brent becomes one of the story’s emotional anchors.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Octavia Spencer in The Help or Melissa Leo in The Fighter a memorable, emotionally specific lift — a supporting part that lands because it carries truth. It offers an actor a chance to make one scene feel like the soul of the movie.

lead_characters.name: Jeremy
lead_characters.demographics: Male, teen to early 20s, white, son, emotionally observant
lead_characters.hook: Jeremy is the son who becomes the family’s quiet adult in the room. He watches Brent more clearly than anyone else and becomes the one person who can still reach him when the rest of the family is at the breaking point.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Lucas Hedges in Manchester by the Sea or Noah Jupe in Honey Boy its emotional precision — a young performer playing intelligence beyond his years. It’s a strong father-son counterpoint role with real tear-jerker potential.

lead_characters.name: Lanna
lead_characters.demographics: Female, teen, white, daughter, emotionally direct
lead_characters.hook: Lanna is the blunt family truth-teller, the child who won’t let Brent hide behind his own mythology. She cuts through the excuses and makes the domestic cost of his obsession impossible to ignore.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of sharp, emotionally honest teen role that gave Kaitlyn Dever in Short Term 12 or Hailee Steinfeld in The Edge of Seventeen real traction. It gives a young actor a chance to play anger, hurt, and love without softening any of it.

lead_characters.name: Carrie
lead_characters.hook: Carrie is the movement-facing version of Brent’s fight: another inventor who has been crushed by the system but still knows how to rally a crowd. She helps turn his private grievance into public action.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of galvanizing supporting role that gives an actor the charge of a movement leader without needing the whole movie on her shoulders. It offers a strong speech scene and a real sense of purpose.

lead_characters.name: Judy
lead_characters.hook: Judy is the reflective counterpoint to the chaos, the one who can turn Brent’s damage into song and meaning. She’s less plot engine than emotional echo, but she gives the story a softer, elegiac register.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do the ‘singing witness’ work of a character like the one in Inside Llewyn Davis or A Star Is Born’s supporting emotional chorus. It’s a compact but memorable showcase if cast with a performer who can carry vulnerability through music.

technical.vfx_details: mostly screen inserts, crowd augmentation, and limited ambulance/shooting aftermath enhancement
technical.sfx_needs: fight choreography, taser hit, gunshot aftermath, medical emergency beats, crowd-control moments

rights_flags.detail: Brent Woods appears to be based on a real inventor and the script is explicitly inspired by real events; life-rights and defamation review are likely needed.
Named public figures and institutions are depicted, including President Reid, Senator Seal, Andy Rancu, and PTAB judges, which raises depiction and clearance review.
Monopoly is explicitly referenced in the payment gag and would need trademark review if retained.
The script repeatedly references the Handy Bar and Car Buddy as product names; if these are real-world products, trademark and factual-clearance review is needed.
The screenplay is inspired by real events and centers on patent litigation and a public legislative campaign; underlying factual rights and legal substantiation should be cleared.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: adult prestige drama with awards-friendly true-story appeal and a mid-to-wide streaming launch path.

budget.note: Contemporary locations keep the spend grounded, but the Capitol rally, courtroom crowd work, multiple company/office spaces, night exteriors, and ambulance/shooting sequence add scope that can creep above a lean indie plan.

casting.note: Brent is a demanding lead: he has to sell charisma, mania, addiction, humiliation, courtroom fire, and late-film vulnerability without losing audience sympathy. Emily and Henry also need actors who can play emotional authority, not just support.

development.note: The script leans heavily on speeches, inventor-club framing, and legal exposition, so the buyer conversation will center on whether the narrative drive stays cinematic through the patent and Capitol material. The inspired-by-real-events lane also means factual substantiation and rights review will matter early.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like true-story prestige dramas about underdogs, legal fights, and damaged but charismatic protagonists.
audience_target.demographics: 35-64 skew, slightly male-leaning but viable for adult women; educated, streaming-native, awards-aware, and responsive to inspirational real-life stories.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary settings and modest VFX keep it in indie territory, but the crowd scenes, courtroom work, and multiple supporting roles push it toward the upper end of the band.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the adult prestige lane: a true-event underdog story with a strong lead role, legal conflict, and a socially legible mission. It is especially attractive to buyers looking for awards-capable material that can be mounted without tentpole economics.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature; the story resolves as a single inventor’s fight and does not present a clean sequel or franchise vector.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Brent is a true showcase role.
strengths.what_it_means: This is the kind of lead that can attract a serious actor looking for a career-resetting performance in the prestige lane. Buyers chasing awards-friendly, emotionally volatile male leads will see immediate value in the range on display.
strengths.evidence: The script moves him from inventor-club comic monologues to breakdown, courtroom fury, addiction, and the Capitol speech.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The Handy Bar gives the story a clean commercial object.
strengths.what_it_means: A simple, visual invention makes the premise easy to grasp and easy to market, which is rare in legal dramas. That clarity helps the movie travel to audiences who want an underdog story they can explain in one sentence.
strengths.evidence: The retirement-center demo, investor pitch, trade-show booth, and courtroom arguments all revolve around the same device.

strengths.what_it_means: The PTAB, IPR, and claim-construction material create a procedural texture that gives the film a real-world edge. Buyers who want prestige material with a fresh institutional arena will notice the specificity.
strengths.evidence: The courtroom scenes, lawyer strategy sessions, and references to claim construction and inter partes review.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The marriage story carries real emotional weight.
strengths.what_it_means: Emily is not just support; she is the cost of the obsession, which gives the film a second emotional engine beyond the patent fight. That broadens the appeal to adult audiences who want the family fallout, not just the business victory.
strengths.evidence: Emily’s garage confrontation, her decision to leave, and the later reconciliation after Brent’s collapse.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The inventor-club framing gives the script a signature voice.
strengths.what_it_means: The recurring storytelling device creates a memorable tonal wrapper and gives the lead a built-in performance arena. That kind of framing can help a buyer see a director’s approach and a star’s showcase in the same package.
strengths.evidence: Brent repeatedly addresses inventor audiences with comic, confessional monologues that reframe the plot.

whats_special.headline: This is a prestige, actor-forward true-story drama with a clean commercial object at its center: one inventor, one device, one fight against a system that wants to erase him. The combination of a showpiece lead role, a legible underdog engine, and a contained contemporary production profile makes it a credible streaming or specialty buy.

items.area: The script leans hard on speechifying.
items.detail: A lot of the emotional and thematic load is carried in inventor-club monologues, courtroom declarations, and explanatory dialogue about patents and mental health. That gives the lead a showcase, but it also means the movie’s momentum depends on dialogue landing as drama, not just information.

items.area: The legal material narrows the audience lane.
items.detail: The PTAB, IPR, claim-construction, and infringement material is specific and credible, but it also makes the middle act feel process-heavy. Buyers will see the prestige upside, but they will also clock that this is not a broad four-quadrant crowd-pleaser.

items.area: Brent is a difficult sympathy balance.
items.detail: He is compelling, but he is also drunk, manic, abusive, and self-sabotaging across multiple stretches, including the marriage collapse and the street fight. That makes the role rich, but it also means the film lives or dies on whether the audience stays with him through some abrasive behavior.

The Capitol rally, congressional speech, and shooting push the film into a bigger political register than the earlier garage-and-courtroom material. That escalation gives the story scale, but it also creates a tonal and budget conversation about how far the movie should travel from its grounded inventor core.

items.area: The inspired-by-real-events lane needs legal care.
items.detail: The script names public figures, institutions, and a real-world patent fight structure, while also dramatizing addiction, misconduct, and corporate wrongdoing. That is manageable for a buyer, but it will trigger factual substantiation and clearance review before anyone gets comfortable.

issues.headline: The main friction is not the premise; it’s the execution load. This is a strong lead role inside a legally specific, speech-driven, true-story drama, which is exactly where buyers will ask how much of the movie is drama and how much is explanation.
